system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2171-04-22 05:53:00 to 2171-04-23 19:58:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with type 1 diabetes, end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, and a history of heart surgery was admitted after presenting with diabetic ketoacidosis and elevated cardiac enzymes indicating a non-ST elevation myocardial infarction. She had no chest pain but was found to have new severe left ventricular dysfunction with an ejection fraction of 19%. A stress test revealed fixed perfusion defects, and cardiac catheterization showed significant coronary artery disease, leading to stent placement in multiple vessels. She was treated for DKA with insulin, managed for acute systolic heart failure with dialysis, and started on dual antiplatelet therapy. A small, asymptomatic arteriovenous fistula was incidentally found and deemed non-interventional. Cellulitis of the right index finger was treated with IV antibiotics, transitioning to oral doxycycline. Her condition stabilized, and she was discharged home with medication adjustments and follow-up plans.
problems: Acute on chronic combined systolic (congestive) and diastolic (congestive) heart failure
Arteriovenous malformation of vessel of lower limb

EXAMINATION:  CTA UPPER EXTREMITY

INDICATION:  ___ year old woman with PAD, chronic b/l hand ischemia  // r/o
vascular inflow lesion. please do runoff b/l upper extremities

TECHNIQUE:  ___ MDCT images were obtained through the upper extremities before,
then after the administration of IV contrast in the arterial and delayed
phases.  Multiplanar reformatted images in coronal and sagittal axis were
generated and reviewed.

COMPARISON:  None.

DOSE:  Total DLP (Body) = 1,019 mGy-cm.

FINDINGS: 

LEFT:  The left subclavian, axillary, and brachial arteries appear to be well
opacified, without evidence of an occlusive embolus.  The left radial and
ulnar arteries are extremely calcified, and given the resolution of CT,
presence of flow cannot be assessed through these arteries, as well as the
arteries of the hand.  Incidental note is made of a left arteriovenous
fistula, which does not demonstrate any flow.

RIGHT:  The right subclavian, axillary, and brachial arteries also appear to
be well opacified, without evidence of an occlusive embolus, although
evaluation of the origin of the right subclavian artery is limited due to
overlying streak artifact.  The right radial and ulnar arteries are extremely
calcified, and again given the resolution of CT, presents flow cannot be
assessed through these arteries, or the arteries of the hand.

CTA CHEST:  The main, lobar, segmental, and subsegmental pulmonary arteries
appear to be well opacified without evidence of a filling defect, concerning
for a pulmonary embolus.

The thyroid is normal.  There is no axillary, hilar, or mediastinal
lymphadenopathy.  The heart size is mildly enlarged.  Note is made of an
artificial mitral valve.  The esophagus is normal without evidence of a hiatal
hernia.

The airways are patent to the subsegmental levels.  No pulmonary nodules
concerning for malignancy identified.  There is no pleural effusion, or
pneumothorax.

The study is not tailored for evaluation of the subdiaphragmatic structures,
however incidental note is made of a 1.4 cm cystic lesion in the pancreatic
head, adjacent to the common bile duct and likely secondary to an IPMN.  There
is evidence of cholelithiasis, without evidence of cholecystitis.

OSSEOUS STRUCTURES:  No lytic or blastic lesions concerning for malignancy are
identified.  Old right-sided rib fractures are identified in the right ___,
___, and 5th ribs.  Central wedging is seen involving the T6, T8, and T9
vertebral bodies, of indeterminate chronicity.


IMPRESSION: 

1.  Arteries in the upper extremities bilaterally appear to be well opacified
through the brachials to the level of the elbow.  Evaluation of the forearm
and wrist is limited, given the heavily calcified vessels.  Presence of flow
cannot be evaluated on this study.  An MRA or Upper extremity angiogram is
recommended for further evaluation of flow.

2.  No evidence of a pulmonary embolus.  No intrathoracic abnormalities
identified.

3.  1.4 cm cystic lesion in the head of the pancreas, statistically most
likely secondary to an IPMN, however can be further evaluated by MRI.

4.  Cholelithiasis.

5.  Occluded left forearm AV fistula.

RECOMMENDATION(S):  Upper extremity angiogram or MRA is recommended to
evaluate for flow in the forearms and hands bilaterally.

NOTIFICATION:  ___ were d/w Dr. ___ at 6pm on the day of the exam by
phone by Dr. ___.

INDICATION:  ___ year old woman with ESRD // please place tunneled HD line

COMPARISON:  CTA ___.

TECHNIQUE:  OPERATORS: Dr. ___ and Dr.
___ radiologist performed the procedure. Dr. ___
supervised the trainee during the key components of the procedure and has
reviewed and agrees with the trainee's findings.
ANESTHESIA: Moderate sedation was provided by administrating divided doses of
50 mcg of fentanyl and 0.5 mg of midazolam throughout the total intra-service
time of 21 minutes during which the patient's hemodynamic parameters were
continuously monitored by an independent trained radiology nurse. 1% lidocaine
was injected in the skin and subcutaneous tissues overlying the access site.
MEDICATIONS: 50 mcg fentanyl, 0.5 mg versed
CONTRAST: 0 ml of Optiray contrast.
FLUOROSCOPY TIME AND DOSE: 1.9 min, 12 mGy

PROCEDURE:  PROCEDURE DETAILS: Following the explanation of the risks,
benefits and alternatives to the procedure, written informed consent was
obtained from the patient. The patient was then brought to the angiography
suite and placed supine on the exam table. A pre-procedure time-out was
performed per ___ protocol. The left upper chest was prepped and draped in
the usual sterile fashion.
Under continuous ultrasound guidance, the patent left internal jugular vein
was compressible and accessed using a micropuncture needle. Permanent
ultrasound images were obtained before and after intravenous access, which
confirmed vein patency. Subsequently a Nitinol wire was passed into the right
atrium using fluoroscopic guidance. The needle was exchanged for a
micropuncture sheath. The Nitinol wire was removed and a short ___ wire was
advanced to make appropriate measurements for catheter length. The ___ wire
was then passed distally into the IVC.
Next, attention was turned towards creation of a tunnel over the upper
anterior chest wall. After instilling superficial and deeper local anesthesia
using lidocaine mixed with epinephrine, a small skin incision was made at the
tunnel entry site. A 23cm tip-to-cuff length catheter was selected. The
catheter was tunneled from the entry site towards the venotomy site from where
it was brought out using a tunneling device. The venotomy tract was dilated
using the introducer of the peel-away sheath supplied. Following this, the
peel-away sheath was placed over the ___ wire through which the catheter was
threaded into the right side of the heart with the tip in the right atrium.
The sheath was then peeled away. The catheter was sutured in place with 0 silk
sutures. Steri-strips were also used to close the venotomy incision site.
Final spot fluoroscopic image demonstrating good alignment of the catheter and
no kinking. The tip is in the right atrium. The catheter was flushed and both
lumens were capped. Sterile dressings were applied. The patient tolerated the
procedure well.

FINDINGS: 

Patent left internal jugular vein.  Final fluoroscopic image showing
hemodialysis catheter with tip terminating in the right atrium.

IMPRESSION: 

Successful placement of a 23cm tip-to-cuff length tunneled dialysis line. The
tip of the catheter terminates in the right atrium. The catheter is ready for
use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Ms. ___ . I’m Dr. ___ , one of the surgical team. You were admitted because of ongoing pain and circulation issues in your left hand related to your dialysis access graft. Do you remember discussing this with your surgeon before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I had that graft placed a while back. It caused hand pain—like coldness, numbness. I was told it might be stealing blood flow. But I didn’t want it removed at the time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. That’s called ‘steal syndrome.’ Your symptoms didn’t get worse, so you kept using it for dialysis. But now there are new ulcers on your left hand, and your right hand is also having circulation problems. We think it’s safer to remove the graft now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So you’re going to take it out? But how will I get dialysis then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do the graft removal today. After that, a temporary dialysis catheter will be placed in your neck so you can continue dialysis safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… I’m nervous about the surgery. Is it risky with my heart and diabetes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed your history—your heart function is stable, and your blood work is within acceptable limits. The surgery is relatively straightforward. We’ll monitor you closely. Your blood pressure and blood sugar will be checked often.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. And my hand—will it get better after the graft is gone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hope so. Removing the graft should improve blood flow to your hand. But we also saw that your arteries are quite calcified, which makes circulation difficult. We’ll get a CT scan today to see exactly what’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had so many scans. Will this one show why my fingers keep cracking and forming scabs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the CT will show the blood vessels in your arms and hands. If there’s poor flow due to blockages, that could explain the ulcers and fissures. We may need to see a hand surgeon later for possible revascularization.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Revascularization? What does that mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means trying to restore blood flow through surgery or a procedure, like opening up narrowed arteries. But we’ll know more after the scan. For now, focus on getting through today’s surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. The surgery went well. We successfully ligated the graft in your left arm. You tolerated it without any issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. My arm feels heavy, but no sharp pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There might be some swelling or bruising. We saw a small hematoma under the dressing, but it’s not concerning. You’ll have a new dialysis line placed tomorrow morning so you can dialyze safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why not today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We wanted to make sure you were stable after surgery. The procedure to place the line requires imaging guidance and a radiology team, which is scheduled for tomorrow at 12 p.m.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the CT scan—did it show anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The larger arteries up to your elbow are open, but the smaller ones in your forearms and hands are heavily calcified. We can’t tell if blood is flowing through them on this type of scan. The hand surgeon reviewed it and thinks you might benefit from a more detailed test later—maybe an MRA.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So my hands won’t heal unless they fix the blood flow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s part of it. Your diabetes and kidney disease also slow healing. But improving circulation could help prevent more ulcers. The hand surgeon will see you as an outpatient to discuss options.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I already lost part of my leg. I don’t want to lose fingers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. That’s why we’re acting now. The graft was likely making things worse. Removing it was the right step. We’ll do everything we can to preserve your hand function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today we’ll place your dialysis catheter in the left side of your neck. It’ll go into the jugular vein and reach your heart. You’ll be given some sedation, and the radiologist will use ultrasound and X-ray to guide it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll feel some pressure and numbing shots, but the sedation will help you relax. Most patients tolerate it well. Afterward, you’ll get dialysis through it, and we’ll make sure it’s working before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—your dialysis catheter was placed successfully. The tip is in the right atrium, and both ports are flowing well. You just finished your dialysis session and did fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t feel much. Just sleepy. Is the catheter permanent?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This one is temporary. Since your left arm graft is gone, your team will decide if you need a new access—maybe in your right arm or leg. That’ll be discussed at your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if everything stays stable. Your hand pain is no worse, you’re eating, and you’ve done dialysis safely through the new line. We’ll send you home with instructions and a follow-up appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us if you develop fever, redness or pus at the incision or catheter site, chest pain, shortness of breath, or if your hand pain worsens. Also, monitor your weight—call if you gain more than 3 pounds in a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue all your usual medicines—insulin, blood pressure pills, aspirin, apixaban, and the others. We’ve sent the updated list to your pharmacy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take tramadol for pain. Is that okay with the other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but take it only as needed. Avoid driving while on it. And don’t take extra acetaminophen—stick to the prescribed dose to protect your liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the hand surgeon appointment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re scheduled for next week. They’ll evaluate whether you’re a candidate for a procedure to improve blood flow to your hands. It’s important to keep that visit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be there. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. A nurse will go over wound care and how to keep the catheter site clean. You’re doing well—just keep following up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your CT also showed gallstones and a small cyst in your pancreas. Nothing urgent, but your primary doctor should follow up on those with an MRI later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: More tests? I’m tired of being poked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. But this is just monitoring. The cyst is likely benign, but we want to make sure it doesn’t change. Your doctor will coordinate it when you’re ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. As long as it’s not surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No surgery planned. Focus on healing your hands and staying on track with dialysis and diabetes care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll have your wheelchair ready shortly, and a nurse will go over your discharge instructions one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready to go home.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with end-stage renal disease, type 2 diabetes, and a history of vascular complications was admitted for left upper extremity pain due to a dialysis graft causing steal syndrome. She underwent successful ligation of the graft and placement of a tunneled hemodialysis catheter in the left internal jugular vein. A CTA showed severe calcification of the radial and ulnar arteries bilaterally, limiting flow assessment, but no central occlusion. Hand surgery recommended outpatient evaluation for possible revascularization. She tolerated dialysis post-procedure, remained stable, and was discharged home with follow-up plans for vascular and surgical care, along with management of chronic conditions including diabetes, heart failure, and peripheral vascular disease.
